implementation_notes: Scala has the holder in the language: 'lazy val author: Author = gateway.find(authorId)' evaluates its right-hand side the first time the value is accessed and caches it - the language specification states exactly that - and Scala 3 implements SIP-20 so the initialization is at most once and no lock is held during the initializer itself. What replaces the classic proxy/holder type is the lazy val, so a single deferred member needs no structure; LazyList covers lazily computed collections, while a def plus an explicit cache or an LRU is the right shape when the value must be refreshed, invalidated or parameterised.
pitfalls: Initialization runs under a lock: a recursive access from inside the initializer (directly or through another lazy val) can deadlock, and heavy I/O there blocks every thread that touches the instance.
The value is cached forever and the initializer captures its inputs, so mutating authorId later leaves a stale author; re-loadable data needs a method or an explicit cache.

For JPA/Hibernate-mapped entities the lazy val does not help: the provider needs proxyable classes with a no-arg constructor, which Scala case classes and val fields complicate - keep the deferral on the domain side or in a mapper.
